notes.title: Start here: two chapters of the Reps upskilling course
notes.body:
This pack comes from the `upskilling/` course inside the jsdrillv2 repository. The app it studies is called Reps: a local drill app that grades your answers and schedules reviews.

Suggested reading order:

1. `upskilling/README.md`, "How to use it". It tells you to keep the cited files open next to each chapter and to read the "Junior vs senior" box last.
2. Chapter 04, "Pure functions and never trusting the client". It is about one grading function used in two places, what the server checks again, and how learner code is run.
3. Chapter 08, "Migrations, seeding and not breaking users". It is about loading course content into the SQLite database without hurting the learner's saved progress.
4. Keep `upskilling/GLOSSARY.md` open for words like idempotent or upsert.

Each chapter names its files at the top. When a sentence mentions a function, open that file and read the function: the quizzes ask about what the code really does, not just what the prose says.

excerpts.quote: **Read one chapter.** Keep the files it cites open next to it.
> Files: `src/lib/grader.ts` (`grade`, `GradeOptions`), `src/app/api/attempts/route.ts` (`checkBody`, `POST`)

readMore.why: The course map: one line per chapter and how to work through them.
Definitions of the vocabulary the chapters use.

notes.title: Core idea: a pure function you can run in two places
notes.body:
A **pure function** gives an output that depends only on its inputs. It does not read a database, the clock or browser globals, and it does not write anything.

Chapter 04 is built around one such function, `grade` in `src/lib/grader.ts`. Before reading the chapter's explanation, find every place in the code that calls `grade` (start with the attempt route and the drill page), and ask yourself why being pure would matter for those particular callers.

The second half of the chapter is a habit worth copying: list honestly what your defence does *not* cover. The chapter has a table of every field the server accepts from the client and whether it can still be abused. Read the route's `checkBody` beside that table and note, field by field, what the server does with each value it receives.

While reading, keep asking two questions: "who decides this value, the client or the server?" and "what happens if the client lies about it?"

excerpts.quote: is a **pure function**. Its output depends only on its inputs. It reads no database, no clock and no global state, and it writes nothing.
The general rule: **the server decides everything that matters, and anything it accepts from the client is either validated or listed as a known limit.**

readMore.why: The grader itself; the header comment states why it is pure.

notes.title: Core idea: content is a cache, user state is precious
notes.body:
Chapter 08 starts by splitting the database file `reps.db` into two kinds of data.

- **Content** (tracks, modules, items, concepts) is written by the course author in `src/content/**`. The database copy can be rebuilt from those files at any time.
- **User state** (attempts, review cards, progress, streaks) only exists in the database.

The chapter says every decision in the seeding script follows from that split. When you read a piece of `seed.ts`, ask: "is this row content or user state?", and then look at exactly which SQL the seeder uses for it: an insert, an upsert that updates, an upsert that leaves the row alone, or an update. Note too how row ids are chosen and what happens to an item that vanished from the content files.

Two words help: **idempotent** means running something once or fifty times leaves the same result. **Foreign keys** link rows in one table to rows in another; check the schema for what each link does when a row is deleted.

excerpts.quote: Every design decision in `seed.ts` follows from one rule: **refresh content freely, and never harm user state.**
Its source of truth *is* the database. It exists nowhere else.

readMore.why: The seeder; its header comment summarises the rules the chapter explains.

notes.title: Why arr.sort() in a solution cannot spoil later tests
notes.body:
**Key: runTests structured-clones each argument with cloneArgs before a call.** In `runTests`, every test call is `invoke(cloneArgs(tc.input), ...)`. `cloneArgs` runs `structuredClone` on each argument, so the solution gets a deep copy. If it sorts that copy in place, the original test input stays as it was for the next test. The only exceptions: functions, and values that cannot be cloned, are passed as they are.

- **Object.freeze**: nothing freezes the inputs; the protection is a copy, not a lock, and `sort()` does not throw.
- **Re-parsed from JSON before each run**: the code clones the inputs it already has; there is no re-parse step.
- **The vm context copies automatically**: the browser runner does not use vm at all (it compiles with `new Function`), and the copy is made explicitly by `cloneArgs`.

excerpts.quote: // Structured-clone the inputs so a mutating solution cannot // corrupt the expectations of later test cases. const result = invoke(cloneArgs(tc.input), TIME_BUDGET_MS - spent);
if (typeof a === "function") return a; try { return structuredClone(a);

readMore.why: Step 4 of "How it works" explains the cloning.

notes.title: What happens to a forged "correct" and "score"
notes.body:
**Key: dropped, because checkBody copies just the allow-listed fields, and the server re-grades.** `checkBody` pulls out five named fields (`itemId`, `response`, `timeSpent`, `mode`, `attempt`) and builds a brand-new object from them. A `correct` or `score` field is never read, so it simply does not exist in what the route uses. The route then calls `grade()` itself and saves its own verdict.

- **Accepted for self-graded kinds**: there is no such branch; the returned object never has a `correct` or `score` field for any kind.
- **400 for unknown fields**: `checkBody` only returns errors for bad required fields (for example a missing `itemId`); extra fields are ignored, not rejected.
- **Stored as the client's claim**: nothing stores them, since they are never copied.

excerpts.quote: const { itemId, response, timeSpent, mode, attempt } = body;
**It has no `correct` and no `score`**, and anything else the client sends is dropped because it is never copied.
// Re-grade server-side rather than trusting the client's verdict.

notes.title: Why progress rows use onConflictDoNothing
notes.body:
**Key: onConflictDoNothing, so a re-seed leaves a learner's level untouched.** The seeder inserts one `user_track_progress` row per track starting at level 1, with `.onConflictDoNothing()`. If the row already exists, the insert does nothing. So a first run creates it, and every later run leaves the learner's real level alone. Content rows are different: they are a cache and get `onConflictDoUpdate`.

- **onConflictDoUpdate**: that would overwrite the stored level with 1 on every re-seed, which is exactly what the chapter says must never happen.
- **Skipped, created lazily by the API**: the seeder does write these rows (lines 408-419).
- **DELETE then INSERT**: that pattern is used only for item-to-concept links, which are content; doing it to progress would wipe the learner's level.

excerpts.quote: // Start every user at level 1 on every track. db.insert(schema.userTrackProgress)
.onConflictDoNothing() .run();
A re-seed must never reset someone's level to 1.

notes.title: What the seeder does with an item removed from content
notes.body:
**Key: it sets is_published = 0 and keeps the row, so history is not cascaded away.** The seeder runs `UPDATE items SET is_published = 0` for built-in items whose id was not seen in this run. The row stays, so the learner's attempts and cards that point at it stay too. Unpublished items drop out of sessions and progress totals, and if the id returns, the upsert publishes it again.

- **Deletes the row and cascades**: that was the *old* behaviour (a hard `DELETE`). The chapter explains it silently erased history, which is why it was replaced.
- **Renames the id with a deleted- prefix**: no code does this; ids are deterministic and never rewritten.
- **Leaves it published**: that is the "no pruning" problem the chapter describes: a removed item would still be scheduled and shown.

excerpts.quote: `UPDATE items SET is_published = 0, updated_at = ? WHERE author_id IS NULL AND is_published = 1
Items that disappear from content are **unpublished, not deleted**. * `attempts` and `user_cards` reference items with ON DELETE CASCADE,

readMore.why: The section "Pruning, and what it cost" tells the hard-delete to soft-delete story.

notes.title: Ticking every option in a multi-select scores 0
notes.body:
**Key: 0, because each false positive cancels a hit and the net is floored at zero.** Work it through `gradeMulti`: there are 2 right options and the learner picked both, so hits = 2. They also picked the 2 wrong options, so falsePositives = 2. `net = Math.max(0, 2 - 2) = 0`. It is not fully correct (there are false positives), so `score = net / rights.length = 0 / 2 = 0`.

- **1**: a score of 1 needs `correct`, which requires `falsePositives === 0`.
- **0.5**: the code never averages over all four options; it subtracts wrong picks from right picks.
- **-0.5**: `Math.max(0, ...)` stops the net from going below zero. The comment says "never negative".

excerpts.quote: const net = Math.max(0, hits - falsePositives); const correct = hits === rights.length && falsePositives === 0; const score = correct ? 1 : rights.length === 0 ? 0 : net / rights.length;
// Each wrong pick cancels one right pick; never negative.

readMore.why: "What purity buys you in tests" shows the same rule on a smaller example.

notes.title: What options.runTests ?? runTests buys the grader
notes.body:
**Key: the server injects the node:vm runner while grader.ts keeps zero node: imports.** `gradeCode` uses `options.runTests` if the caller passed one, and otherwise the default browser `runTests`. The API route passes `serverGradeOptions` (the vm runner); the browser passes nothing. So the grader never needs to import `node:vm` itself, which keeps it bundleable for the browser, and a unit test can hand in a fake runner. The chapter calls this "dependency injection at the smallest useful size".

- **Detects Node vs browser at runtime**: the opposite: the chapter says letting the grader find out where it runs would make it impure, so the caller decides.
- **Learners supply their own runner**: the option is set by the route and scripts, not by anything in a learner's submission.
- **Makes grading asynchronous**: `run(...)` is called and its result used directly; nothing is awaited or streamed.

excerpts.quote: const run = options.runTests ?? runTests;
It keeps `grader.ts` free of any `node:` import, so it still bundles for the browser, and it lets a unit test pass in a fake runner.
Rather than letting the grader find out where it is running (which would make it impure), the difference is passed in:

notes.title: Why the server cannot catch a false attempt: 1
notes.body:
**Key: the first miss on a retryable item is not posted, so nothing contradicts it.** The server re-grades the *answer*, but whether this was a second try is something only the client knows. The first wrong try is never sent to the server, so the server has no record to compare against. A client that sends `attempt: 1` therefore escapes the 0.5 cap that `attempt === 2` applies. The route's "Trust boundary" comment names this as an accepted risk and gives the fix: post the first miss.

- **The route looks up the earlier attempt row**: there is no earlier row to find, because the miss was never posted.
- **The grader spots second tries from the response**: `grade()` sees only the item and the response; the route sets `verdict.attempt` from the client field.
- **attempt is ignored**: it is used: `attempt === 2` caps the score at 0.5.

excerpts.quote: The * first miss is never posted, so there is nothing server-side to * check it against; a client that always sends `attempt: 1` gets full * credit for second-try successes.
if (attempt === 2) { verdict.attempt = 2; if (verdict.correct) verdict.score = Math.min(verdict.score, 0.5);

readMore.why: The table "What the server still trusts" lists this and the other client inputs.

notes.title: Why an infinite loop stops on the server
notes.body:
**Key: runInContext gets a timeout, which V8 enforces even partway through the loop.** On the server each test call is `call.runInContext(context, { timeout: limit })`. Node's `vm` timeout is enforced by the JavaScript engine (V8) while the code is still running, so even `while (true) {}` is cut off after the budget. The thrown error is turned into a `TimeoutError`, which becomes an ordinary timeout verdict.

- **No while keyword in the context**: the vm context limits which globals exist, not the language syntax; the loop compiles fine and runs until the timeout.
- **Next.js aborts the handler**: the chapter says that before the vm runner, an infinite loop "froze the whole API"; nothing in Next.js stopped it.
- **A worker thread terminated after 2 seconds**: a terminable `worker_threads` worker is listed only as a future option; today the code runs on the server's own thread.

excerpts.quote: return call.runInContext(context, { timeout: limit }); } catch (e) { if (isVmTimeout(e)) throw new TimeoutError(limit);
V8 enforces that timeout **mid-loop**, so `while (true) {}` stops after `TIME_BUDGET_MS` (2 seconds).
It also still runs on the server's own thread and heap

notes.title: How a forged timeSpent still nudges scheduling
notes.body:
**Key: a tiny time on a correct, previously-seen review earns Easy, pushing it further out.** The route clamps `timeSpent` to 0..3600, which stops absurd values but not lies inside that range. `ratingFor` gives `Easy` when the answer is correct, `timeSpent < budget * 0.5`, and `reps > 0` (seen before). So a client claiming 1 second turns a Good into an Easy, and the next review is scheduled later.

- **A huge value overflows the interval**: the clamp caps it at 3600, and a slow time leads to `Hard`, not a date in the past.
- **A negative value is stored and resets the card**: `Math.max(0, ...)` turns a negative value into 0.
- **No effect, the server measures time**: the route uses the client's `timeSpent`; its own comment lists this as a trusted input.

excerpts.quote: timeSpent: isFiniteNumber(timeSpent) ? Math.round(Math.max(0, Math.min(timeSpent, MAX_TIME_SPENT))) : undefined,
// Fast, confident, and not the first time seeing it. if (timeSpent < budget * 0.5 && reps > 0) return Rating.Easy;
if (timeSpent > budget * 1.6) return Rating.Hard;
clamped to 0..3600s, but a small value can still turn * a Good into an Easy.

notes.title: Why the browser time budget cannot stop while (true)
notes.body:
**Key: nothing, because the check runs after the call returns, so the tab simply hangs.** In the browser runner the budget is compared only after `invoke(...)` returns. JavaScript runs one thing at a time on a thread, so a loop that never ends never gives control back, and the check is never reached. The budget does catch code that is slow but finishes. Stopping a runaway loop in the browser would need a Web Worker that can be terminated.

- **Interrupts the loop after 2 seconds**: that is what the *server* vm runner does; the browser code cannot interrupt itself.
- **A setTimeout throws a TimeoutError**: a timer callback cannot run while the loop holds the thread, so it could never interrupt it.
- **new Function detects the loop**: compiling only checks syntax; `while (true) {}` is valid code.

excerpts.quote: JavaScript cannot interrupt a synchronous function from the same * thread. In the **browser** (the default `compile`, via `new Function`) * an infinite loop therefore still hangs the tab: `TIME_BUDGET_MS` is * checked only *after* a call returns
// Only reached if the call returned — see the header comment. if (spent > TIME_BUDGET_MS) return timeoutVerdict(tc, spent);

notes.title: Why item ids are item-<authored id>, not a UUID
notes.body:
**Key: so a re-seed upserts the same row and history keeps pointing at it.** `seed()` builds each item's id from the text item- plus the author's own id. Every run produces the same id for the same item, so the upsert updates that row instead of creating a new one. The learner's `user_cards` and `attempts` refer to the item by id, so they keep pointing at the right thing. The cost: an authored id becomes permanent, like a database primary key.

- **better-sqlite3 cannot use UUID keys**: the chapter's reason is about keeping history attached, not a driver limit.
- **Faster without randomness**: speed is never the argument; a fresh UUID per run would break every link to user history.
- **Renaming migrates history automatically**: the opposite: a rename looks like one removal plus one new item, and the new one starts with a fresh card.

excerpts.quote: const itemId = `item-${item.id}`;
With deterministic ids, "the item `js-async-retry`" is the same row forever, so the learner's card for it survives any number of content edits.
Rename `js-async-retry` to `js-retry` and the seeder sees one removal and one new item.

notes.title: Why it matters that grade() is pure
notes.body:
**Key: the same function runs in the browser and on the server, so the two stay in step.** Because `grade()` depends only on its inputs, it runs unchanged in the browser (instant feedback, even offline) and in the API route (the grade that is actually stored). Both sides run the very same code, so they cannot drift apart. The same purity lets the content checker script reuse the production grader.

- **Lets the server skip its re-grade**: the opposite: the route always re-grades rather than trusting the client's verdict.
- **Needed to run inside a transaction**: the chapter never links purity to database transactions; a pure grader does not touch the database at all.
- **React memoizes pure functions**: the chapter gives no such reason, and the server-side grade does not run inside React at all.

excerpts.quote: Runs client-side for instant feedback and again on the server when * the attempt is recorded, so a tampered client cannot inflate a score.
A grader that read `Date.now()`, the DB or `window` could not run unchanged in both places. And since both sides run the same function, they cannot drift apart.
// Re-grade server-side rather than trusting the client's verdict.

notes.title: Four more chapters: types, bugs, learning design and testing
notes.body:
The newer questions draw on four more chapters of the same course.

Chapter 02 is about modelling eight kinds of question in TypeScript: how the item, response and grade types are shaped, where the types stop checking, and how the variant data is stored. Chapter 05 is a casebook of real bugs found while verifying the rebuild, each with a symptom, a fix and a lesson. Chapter 06 turns memory research into code: the review scheduler, how an answer becomes a rating, how a session is assembled, and how progress is measured. Chapter 07 explains how the app was tested in layers without ever opening a browser.

Read each chapter's "Junior vs senior" box last, as the README suggests, and keep the cited source files open: many questions turn on one specific line of code or prose.

excerpts.quote: Reps was built in a terminal, with no browser automation available.
Every bug here was real, and each was found by *verifying* the work before commit, not by a user.

readMore.why: Scheduling, ratings and sessions as encoded learning claims.

notes.title: Why a class hierarchy fails for serialised items
notes.body:
Chapter 02 lists two textbook failure modes for modelling the eight item kinds. The second is a class hierarchy such as `McqItem extends Item`. It is awkward to serialise to JSON and awkward to send across the server/client boundary, and its `instanceof` checks stop working once the value has been through `JSON.parse`, because parsing yields plain objects, not class instances.

- Table-per-kind storage is a separate decision about the database, discussed later in the chapter.
- Narrowing is not the complaint; the chapter's answer is a discriminated union on a literal `kind`.
- Shared fields are what a base class would give you, so that is not the problem either.

excerpts.quote: needs `instanceof` checks that stop working once the value has been through `JSON.parse`.

notes.title: One declaration, a runtime array and a type
notes.body:
`ITEM_KINDS` is declared once with `as const`, and `ItemKind` is derived from it. That gives a runtime array and a compile-time type from the same source. The array lets the app iterate, and `ITEM_KIND_META: Record<ItemKind, …>` must contain every kind or the build fails. The type lets a `switch` over kinds be exhaustive.

- `as const` makes the array readonly to the compiler; it does not install runtime traps.
- Nothing here reaches the database schema.
- The array survives the build, which is the reason it exists.

excerpts.quote: A runtime array and a compile-time type, from one declaration.

notes.title: Grade: a required core with optional extras
notes.body:
`Response` is a true discriminated union, but `Grade` takes a different approach on purpose: one type with two required fields, `correct` and `score`, plus optional detail fields. The reason is who reads it. Consumers such as `ratingFor`, the attempts table and the session summary only need `correct` and `score`; the details are read only by the feedback UI for the kind that produced them.

- Storage format is not the reason given.
- The grader does not need casts to return a Grade; the casts in chapter 02 are on payloads.
- Grades are computed by the server's own re-grade, not taken from the client.

excerpts.quote: **Put the fields every consumer needs in the required core, and the per-variant fields in optional extras.**

notes.title: Where the types cheat, and what holds the line
notes.body:
In `Item`, `kind` and `payload` are not correlated, so an item with `kind: "code"` and an `McqPayload` compiles, and the grader has to cast payloads. Each cast is a promise the compiler cannot check. It holds for two reasons: the DSL is the only producer of items and always pairs a kind with its payload, and `scripts/check-content.ts` grades every item against its own answer.

- `toItem()` uses a plain `JSON.parse`; the chapter says a validated parse step would be needed if you correlated the types.
- `ItemOf<K, P>` is a sketch for exercise 2, not the shipped type.
- SQLite will store any JSON; the database cannot enforce the shape.

excerpts.quote: So the correlation is enforced by construction and by test, not by the type system.

notes.title: A total grader: wrong-kind input is just a wrong answer
notes.body:
The fill-blank case reads `response.kind === "fill-blank" ? response.values : {}`. An mcq response therefore reaches `gradeBlanks` as an empty set of values and grades as wrong. Nothing throws. Chapter 02 calls this keeping the grader total: every input produces a `Grade`. That matters because the server runs the grader on untrusted input from the client.

- No exception is raised, so there is no error status to report.
- The grader does not reinterpret a choice id as a blank value.
- It always returns a Grade, never null.

excerpts.quote: That keeps the grader total: every input produces a `Grade`.

notes.title: No default: let the compiler list the work
notes.body:
`grade()` returns `Grade` and switches over all eight kinds with no `default`. Add a ninth kind to `ITEM_KINDS` and TypeScript reports that the function lacks an ending return statement. The same happens in `emptyResponse`, `ITEM_KIND_META` and every other exhaustive switch, so the compiler hands you the full to-do list. A `default` returning a wrong grade would silently hide all of it.

- Without a default nothing falls through quietly; the build fails first.
- check-content runs later and is not what flags the new kind.
- The chapter's rule is the opposite of adding a default: don't add one to a switch over a closed union.

excerpts.quote: **Don't add a default to a switch over a closed union.**

notes.title: When a JSON column is the right trade
notes.body:
Chapter 02 is honest about the cost of a JSON `payload` column: the database cannot enforce its shape, and you cannot efficiently query inside it. JSON still wins because payloads are written by exactly one trusted path, the seeder working from DSL-validated content, and are always read whole. The DSL assertions and the content linter supply the integrity the database gives up.

- User-authored items are the case where the chapter says the balance would tip the other way.
- The comparison table credits per-kind tables with foreign keys and NOT NULL, so that is not the argument.
- The table says the opposite about querying: normal SQL works for per-kind tables, not inside JSON.

excerpts.quote: payloads are **written by exactly one trusted path**

notes.title: A checker that could not fail
notes.body:
`JSON.stringify` turns a function inside an array into `null`, so the stored retry test called the learner's code with `(null, 3)`. The first check round-tripped the tests and compared `JSON.stringify` of the result with `JSON.stringify` of the originals. Both sides go through the same serialiser and lose the function in exactly the same way, so the strings are always equal and the check never fires.

- `JSON.parse` handles `null` without complaint; nothing crashed.
- The check did see the data, just after it had already been flattened.
- The comparison was a strict `!==` between two identical strings.

excerpts.quote: Both sides go through `JSON.stringify`, so both lose the function in exactly the same way.

notes.title: Inspect the originals, and verify your verifier
notes.body:
The real fix for bug 5b, `findUnserialisable()`, walks the original values before serialisation can hide anything and names the first value JSON would drop: a function, a symbol, a bigint, a Map and so on. The retry item itself was rewritten to build its flaky function inside a harness from plain numbers.

The general lesson is to verify your verifier: before trusting a new check, feed it the exact bug it should catch and watch it go red.

- Test data still lives as JSON in the database; the fix is in the checker.
- Comparing parsed values cannot work, because parsing happens after the function is gone.
- `JSON.stringify` does not throw on functions; it silently drops them.

excerpts.quote: Before you trust a new check, make it fail on purpose

notes.title: The roadmap that could never open
notes.body:
Level 2 used to unlock when level-1 cards reached a stability of at least 7 days. In FSRS, stability only grows when reviews happen across real elapsed time, so a learner who got everything right in one sitting had modest stabilities and stayed locked out for weeks. Unit tests missed it because every function was individually correct. An end-to-end progression script found it: it answered every level-1 item through the real `POST /api/attempts` and expected `unlocked: { level: 2 }`.

- Accuracy per day was never the rule.
- No learner report or type error was involved; verification caught it before users did.

excerpts.quote: **stability only grows when reviews happen across real elapsed time**

notes.title: Write the linter for your own parser's limits
notes.body:
`renderMarkdown()` is hand-written and handles inline code with a single regex, which has no notion of doubled or nested backticks. Two explanations rendered as garbled prose. The content was corrected, and a permanent lint, `checkProse()` in `scripts/check-content.ts`, now fails on doubled backticks, an odd backtick count and nested backticks in every rendered string.

- The hand-rolled renderer stays; choosing a subset is described as a legitimate trade.
- The regex itself was not changed to escape doubled runs.
- No visual snapshot test exists; the guard is at the input.

excerpts.quote: **When you write your own parser, write the linter for its limits.**

notes.title: Tests must construct their preconditions
notes.body:
The primer assertion needed an item from a module the learner had never touched. It sampled a mixed session and hoped one would be there. On a fresh database that was nearly always true, but the scripts record real attempts, and on a well-drilled database a mixed session may hold only reviews. The result depended on the database's history, not the code. The fix asks `/api/cheatsheet` for every module, picks one with `seenItems` 0, requests a module-mode session for it, and prints an honest skip when none is left.

- Server start-up timing was not the cause.
- The render-purity fixes belong to bug 5f.
- The port incident belongs to 5g.

excerpts.quote: **Tests must construct their preconditions, not hope for them.**

notes.title: A second try earns half credit and a Hard rating
notes.body:
For retryable kinds a first miss eliminates the wrong choice and allows one more try. The server enforces the scoring in `POST /api/attempts`: on attempt 2 a correct verdict's score is capped with `Math.min(score, 0.5)`, and the rating is forced to Hard instead of the usual speed-based `ratingFor`. Chapter 06 explains: a near miss is worth more than a peek and less than knowing it, so the card comes back soon.

- Full credit would treat a retry like fluency, which the chapter rejects.
- It is not recorded as a miss; giving up is what records the first response as a miss.
- Time does not lift a second-try success to Good.

excerpts.quote: **a near miss is worth more than a peek and less than knowing it.**

notes.title: How a mixed session is filled
notes.body:
`buildSession()` in mixed mode works in steps. First come overdue reviews, most overdue first, up to `reviewBudget = Math.ceil(size * 0.6)`. Then new items from unlocked levels fill the rest; module- and level-scoped sessions skip the level gate because the learner asked for them. If the session is still short, seen but not-yet-due items fill it, shuffled. Finally items are interleaved by track.

- New items come second, not first.
- There is no separate low-accuracy step in mixed mode; weak mode is the one that spends everything on reviews.
- Seen, not-due items are only the last filler.

excerpts.quote: `reviewBudget = Math.ceil(size * 0.6)`, taking the most overdue cards first

notes.title: Mastery and unlocking answer different questions
notes.body:
`masteryScore()` weights retention (from stability) at 0.7 and accuracy at 0.3, averaged over every item in scope with unseen items counting 0, so coverage is built in. Chapter 06 keeps this display metric apart from the unlock gate, which uses coverage and accuracy. They answer different questions: how durable is what you know, versus are you ready for the next material.

- Retention dominates mastery; accuracy only stops a lucky guess reading as mastery.
- It is the other way round: the gate deliberately avoids stability.
- Where the metric is computed is not the argument.

excerpts.quote: "how durable is what you know?" versus "are you ready for the next material?"

notes.title: Negative cases are what let a linter fail
notes.body:
`check-content.ts` runs the production grader against each item's own answer key, and wherever it can it checks both directions: the right answer passes and a wrong answer fails. Chapter 07 explains why. A grader that returned `correct: true` for everything would pass every positive-only check. The negative cases are what make the linter able to fail, which is bug 5b's lesson applied systematically.

- The linter uses the real grader; negative cases do not replace it.
- Warnings versus problems is a separate distinction about blocking.
- Unit tests exist alongside the linter; it does not stand in for them.
